notes:
I checked mainly older commentaries on biblehub.com and studylight.org (Gill, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Matthew Henry, Calvin, Wesley, Keil & Delitzsch, Haydock), plus preceptaustin.org and Enduring Word. I didn't find any Orthodox, netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org or prosperity / word-of-faith / hyper-grace material on this passage, so those are left out.

**Overview (vv. 1–21)**
- Matthew Henry blames the lust of the eye, and the pride of life, and says the tribes put their own convenience ahead of the good of the whole people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/32-1.htm
- Enduring Word (David Guzik, from the Calvary Chapel stream) says Moses feared their complacency would discourage the other tribes, as the unfaithful spies had done forty years before. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-32/
- Whedon says the request looked to Moses selfish and divisive. It went against the command to divide the land by lot (Num 26:55), seemed to doubt the conquest, and set a bad precedent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-32.html

**v. 1:** Ellicott says these two tribes had camped next to each other for 38 years, so it was natural they wanted to live near each other. He notes Jazer had rich pasture and Gilead was very fertile. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-32.html
- Precept Austin points out that Reuben is named first only here, as firstborn. After this Gad comes first, because Gad clearly leads. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-32-commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary's sermon notes compare their thinking to Lot's choice in Genesis 13:10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/32.htm

**v. 2:** Gill, following Aben Ezra, suggests Gad came up with the plan and talked Reuben into it while the two were camped side by side. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/32-2.htm
- Constable thinks Gad comes first because it was the more important tribe (cf. Gen 49:4). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-32.html

**v. 3:** Keil & Delitzsch think Jazer is named first because it had especially good pasture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/32-2.htm
- Haydock (Catholic) says Sebam and Nebo were later taken back by Moab (Isa 15), and Beon may be Baal-meon (Josh 13:17). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html
- Whedon says Nebo was the name of a pagan god, so it would naturally be renamed after the conquest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-32.html

**v. 4:** Precept Austin notes that the whole nation had already conquered this land, so these tribes wouldn't have to fight for it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-32-commentary
- The Biblical Illustrator calls it ingratitude: they wanted land all Israel had fought for, without fighting further themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/numbers-32.html

**v. 5:** Ellicott says "do not make us cross" could just mean "give us land in the east." But Moses took it, probably correctly, as asking to leave the conquest of Canaan to the others. Either way the words were selfish and would dishearten the rest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-32.html
- Haydock sees them as a picture of people who want heaven without effort, citing 2 Timothy 2:5. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html
- Guzik quotes Wenham: settling outside the land promised to Abraham showed a troubling indifference to God's word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/numbers/numbers-32.cfm

**v. 6:** Wesley explains "sit here" as staying in ease and peace while their brothers fight a bloody war. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/numbers-32.html
- The Biblical Illustrator applies it to the church: if one Christian may stay out of church fellowship, so may all, and there would be no visible church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/numbers-32.html

**v. 7:** Ellicott says the verb for "discourage" really means "alienate" or "turn away." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-32.html
- Haydock notes that Deuteronomy 3 tells the same story without these rebukes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html

**vv. 8–9:** Enduring Word: the wilderness generation lacked the faith to enter and chose to stay put, and Moses feared the same unbelief here. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-32/
- The Pulpit sermon notes argue that if ten spies could turn all Israel, the desertion of two whole tribes was far more dangerous. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/32.htm

**vv. 10–11:** Haydock notes that Hebrew oaths are often left unfinished, so the literal sense is "surely none shall see…." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html

**v. 12:** Ellicott points back to Numbers 14:24. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-32.html
- On "Kenizzite," Wesley says Caleb was named after his grandfather Kenaz. Haydock gives an alternative: Caleb may have taken the title from Kenizzite land promised to him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/numbers-32.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html

**v. 13:** Ellicott sees the fulfilment of Numbers 14:33–34. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-32.html
- Haydock notes the Greek Old Testament says God "rolled them over," picturing their hardships. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html

**v. 14:** The Cambridge Bible calls "brood" an insult used in anger, a word found nowhere else in the Old Testament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/32-14.htm
- Calvin reads it as "filling up the measure" of their fathers (Jesus' phrase), adding fuel to God's anger. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/32-14.html
- Gill: like fathers, like sons. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/32-14.html
- Enduring Word cites a writer who hears an early echo of Jesus' "brood of vipers" (Matt 12:34; 3:7). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-32/
- Pulpit is the dissenting voice. It says Moses' harsh words were excused by how things looked but not justified by what was really happening. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/32-14.htm

**v. 15:** Wesley: "all this people" means the others who would follow their example and refuse to cross. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/numbers-32.html
- Precept Austin notes that this time no limit is put on the wilderness stay, unlike the earlier 40 years. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-32-commentary
- Haydock says God had decreed that all should conquer together. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html

**v. 16:** Whedon thinks they came back after talking it over with their tribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-32.html
- Ellicott: sheepfolds were usually loose stone walls, and "build" cities probably means repair them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-32.html

**v. 17:** Ellicott: "little ones" covers everyone who couldn't defend themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-32.html
- Wesley suggests not every man went, only as many as were needed, with some left to guard the families. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/numbers-32.html
- Haydock gives the numbers: 70,580 stayed, 40,000 went (Josh 4:13). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html

**v. 18:** Enduring Word: they promised to fight until the conquest was complete, which answered the worry about discouraging the others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-32/

**v. 19:** Ellicott says this isn't defiance. They are simply giving up any claim west of the Jordan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-32.html
- Expositor's Bible asks how they could know their inheritance had "come to them" before any division. Its answer: they had already made up their minds. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-32.html

**v. 20:** Wesley and Ellicott connect "before the LORD" with the ark. Reuben and Gad marched just ahead of it, and Israel crossed the Jordan in front of it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/numbers-32.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-32.html
- Haydock reads it as under God's guidance and protection. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html

**v. 21:** Precept Austin quotes the UBS handbook. The tribes had offered to go "before the Israelites," but Moses changes it to "before the LORD," making the conquest a matter of faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-32-commentary
- Haydock says "every man" means as many as were needed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html

**Where readers differ**
I found no real split between Protestant traditions. Wesley (Methodist), Calvin (Reformed, via Henry), Gill (Baptist) and Guzik all read the request as selfish. The real difference is over how harshly to judge the tribes:
- **Mostly against them:** Precept Austin calls stopping short of the Jordan a mistake driven by worldly motives. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-32-commentary
- **More generous:** another writer quoted there says they were only asking the Lord to provide, not complaining, and they did keep their promise. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-32-commentary
- **Later history:** Ellicott and Wesley note these tribes were among the first taken captive by Assyria. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/numbers-32.html
- **Lost fellowship:** Expositor's says they won good land but lost close ties with the other tribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-32.html

**Catholic reading:** Haydock agrees with the traditional reading and adds the "heaven without effort" picture in v. 5. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-32.html
